title: The Iron Age Queen Who Helped Bring Britain to its Knees - Nautilus
gist: Archaeologist Miles Russell argues in his book 'Caratacus: Great King of Britain' that Verica, the exiled Atrebates client king of Rome whose ouster gave Claudius his pretext to invade Britain around 40 CE, was actually a woman — the daughter, not son, of Commius.

insights.claim: Verica ruled the Atrebates of southern Britain in the early first century as a Roman client king allied with Emperor Claudius, giving Rome a foothold on the island.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Client-state arrangements as a foothold for later intervention is a recurring geopolitical pattern.

insights.claim: According to Roman historian Cassius Dio, Verica's exile around 40 CE gave Claudius a pretext to invade Britain, starting the campaign that led to the Roman conquest.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Exiled allies as invasion pretexts is a classic template for great-power intervention.
insights.quote: it offered a pretext for Claudius to invade Britain

insights.claim: Archaeologist Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues in his new book that Verica was a female king, the daughter rather than the son of Commius.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows how canonical historical narratives can rest on unexamined assumptions in ancient sources.
insights.quote: King Verica wasn’t the son of Commius, she was the daughter of Commius—Verica was a female king.
